newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Dancer Cortes takes flamenco into the pop age.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Dancer Cortes takes flamenco into the pop age.

text.p: Madonna, Michael Jackson and Prince want to make videos with him. Giorgio Armani designs his troupe's costumes.

From the moment he strides on stage, bare-chested, long-haired and wearing a black skirt, it's clear that Spanish sensation Joaquin Cortes is revolutionising the traditional music and dance of the gypsies of Andalusia.
"I am the first modern gypsy. I am not just flamenco. I am Joaquin Cortes," he declares. "What I do is new and no one else is doing it."
The 27-year-old has been feted like a rock star and lauded in glossy magazines like "Vogue" and "Vanity Fair".

His "Gypsy Passion" show has thrilled audiences across Europe and the Americas with a display of high energy, innovation and sexuality. Cortes and his 11 dancers and 14 musicians blend ballet and avant garde, jazz and blues, African and Oriental music to flamenco's gypsy and Moorish hybrid.
Some purists say he is degrading flamenco by popularising it. That does not worry the diminutive but irrepressibly confident Cortes.
"I don't consider myself just a dancer, let alone a flamenco dancer," he said after an afternoon rehearsal for a sold-out show in Miami.
"I am an integral artist. I love movies, I love fashion, I love music. I dance for young people."
Flamenco has not changed for decades, he said.
"I like to explore and to experiment."
His show in Miami, the most Hispanic of U.S. cities, was part of a brief American tour which also included New York, Chicago and Los Angeles.

The crowd whooped with delight as he made his dramatic entrance. After two hours of dance and music which moved from the brooding to the exhilarating, the auditorium was in a frenzy as Cortes, sweat glistening from his torso, soaked up the applause.
"I don't see him as a dancer," said his producer, Pino Sagliocco. "I am treating him like a rock star."

Born in Cordoba, Cortes was raised by his grandfather in a working-class district of Madrid. He frequented the flamenco clubs, or tablaos, and entered the school of the National Ballet of Spain when he was 12. He joined its troupe at age 15 but left in 1990 to form his own company.

He is already a superstar in Spain, where his popularity with the young mirrors that of the new wave of bullfighters such as Jesulin, who has himself appeared in a video with Madonna. During a summer tour he performed in bullrings and at the famous San Fermin festival in Pamplona.
He has appeared in Carlos Suara's documentary "Flamenco" and Pedro Almodovar's "The Flower of My Secret". He would like to make more films, he says.
"My status as a big star is because my work is totally new," he said.

Even if the performance veered close at times to a pastiche of Michael Jackson, some of the most stirring moments of "Gypsy Passion" were the old flamenco of blood-curdling laments, frenetic guitars and twirling dancers.
One highlight was the Romance Amargo (Bitter Romance), a portrayal of a gypsy knifefight inspired by the murder of poet Federico Garcia Lorca by Fascists in 1936.
"'Gypsy Passion' tells the history of the gypsy, who has been repressed, expelled from countries, persecuted and maltreated," said Cortes. "The shout of freedom of this race was dance and song."
